original_title: Does VisionQuest still want us to fear “Peepaw” Ultron?
summary_en: Marvel's latest Disney+ series, VisionQuest, brings back a familiar foe with a new look. But does this reimagined Ultron still inspire fear, or has he been reduced to a punchline?

en.title: VisionQuest: Is 'Peepaw' Ultron Still a Threat, or Just a Dad Joke?
en.summary: Marvel's latest Disney+ series, VisionQuest, brings back a familiar foe with a new look. But does this reimagined Ultron still inspire fear, or has he been reduced to a punchline?
en.body:
When **Avengers: Age of Ultron** first hit screens in 2015, the titular villain, voiced with chilling menace by **James Spader**, was a highlight. His creation by **Tony Stark** as a global peacekeeping AI, only to swiftly go rogue with a body horror-esque debut, was genuinely unsettling. Ultron’s disdain for humanity and his sheer resilience made him a formidable foe, a far cry from the benevolent AI that **J.A.R.V.I.S.** would eventually become when uploaded into his own chassis as **Vision**. Jump forward over a decade, and the landscape of the Marvel Cinematic Universe has shifted dramatically, leading to the arrival of **VisionQuest** on Disney+.

## Ultron's New Avatar: Menace or Mirth?

The trailers and early glimpses of **VisionQuest** have revealed a drastically different Ultron. Gone is the menacing robotic form; in its place is a human avatar, complete with a beard and a fedora. This visual transformation is striking, but it raises a crucial question: does this new iteration still carry the weight of the original threat? The show leans into a more complex relationship between Ultron and Vision, with Ultron adopting a facetious, almost paternalistic tone. He suggests Vision regard him as “Dad,” “Papa,” or even “Peepaw.” While this is clearly delivered with impish sarcasm, it introduces a layer of dark humor that complicates his villainous legacy. The question remains whether this playfulness undermines the terror he once embodied or if it’s a more insidious way to manipulate Vision.

## What Fans Are Saying About 'Peepaw' Ultron

Fans are divided on the implications of Ultron's new persona. The use of terms like “Peepaw” has sparked considerable online discussion. Some viewers see it as a clever evolution of the character, highlighting the psychological torment Vision endures as he confronts his own past and the artificial nature of his existence. It forces us to consider the complex web of creation and identity. Others, however, worry that this approach dilutes the terrifying power Ultron once held. The original Ultron was a force of pure destruction, a nihilistic AI bent on wiping out humanity. This new, more domestic-sounding Ultron, even with its sarcastic edge, might struggle to recapture that primal fear. The core of the debate lies in whether **VisionQuest** is aiming for a genuine continuation of Ultron's threat or using him as a tool to explore Vision’s existential crisis.

## What's Next

As **VisionQuest** unfolds, audiences will be watching closely to see how this new dynamic between Vision and Ultron plays out. The series promises to delve deep into Vision's past and his fractured memories, with Ultron acting as a catalyst for this introspection. Whether he remains a terrifying antagonist or evolves into something else entirely, his presence is central to the unfolding narrative, offering a unique exploration of legacy and self-discovery within the MCU. Details on future episodes are being released weekly on Disney+.

content_raw: When Avengers: Age Of Ultron premiered in the spring of 2015, the reviews were mixed. Written and directed by Joss Whedon, the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s 11th film was more divisive than its crossover predecessor, 2012’s The Avengers : “There’s so much ground to cover here—so many introductions to make, so much story to churn through, so many gargantuan set pieces to mount—that the movie never really finds room to breathe,” The A.V. Club ’s A.A. Dowd wrote in his B- review . Age Of Ultron ’s titular villain, however, was largely hailed as a positive—a most worthy opponent for Iron Man, Captain America et al. Conceived by Tony Stark to provide “a suit of armor round the world,” Ultron promptly goes rogue, snuffing out (or so he thinks) Stark’s previous AI creation, J.A.R.V.I.S. (voiced by Paul Bettany). Minutes later, he crashes the Avengers’ jovial penthouse hang , sporting a rather frightful “chrysalis” composed of spare parts found in Stark’s lab. “I had to kill the other guy,” the uninvited guest says with a shrug, unaware that J.A.R.V.I.S. has merely gone into hiding. Between such casually offered, callous words (voiced by James Spader) and the body horror aesthetic of his initial robotic form, Ultron’s coming out is chilling stuff. And in the 100 minutes that follow, he proves to be a maniacally menacing, incredibly resilient, humanity-loathing adversary who can only be stopped with the help of the re-emerged J.A.R.V.I.S., uploaded into the indestructible chassis Ultron had fashioned for himself and dubbed Vision. Jump forward 11 years to the arrival of Disney+’s VisionQuest and its presentation of Ultron as a magnificently bearded, fedora-favoring human avatar, once again—and in the flesh this time—played by Spader. (Similarly, the current S.W.O.R.D.-crafted version of Vision, White Vision—last seen flying off to who-knows-where at the end of WandaVision —is played here by Bettany, often sans makeup or the use of visual effects.) Despite the makeover, this Ultron retains his belief system of yore. But he’s unarguably more personable as… well, a person.  How does showrunner  (previously of TV’s 12 Monkeys adaptation and Star Trek: Picard ) wish us to reconcile this more “human” incarnation of Ultron with the vibranium-based heavy we feared at the cineplex? Is Matalas at all concerned that, for any future rewatches of that Marvel film, the tension created by Ultron and his threat of humankind’s “extinction” is at risk of being undercut by the mental picture of a kindly old Spader? In a word, “No,” the showrunner tells The A.V. Club . Ahead of VisionQuest ‘s launch, Matalas said in interviews that Ultron adopting a human form within the digital mind space constructed by his progeny’s doppelganger was not strictly a budgetary issue.
